messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 22
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Auditor
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 43

He works in a cubicle on the fifteenth floor, staring at spreadsheets that blur into grey rectangles. Numbers that once aligned neatly for him now drift apart, decimal points sliding out of place. He catches himself recalculating the same column three, four times, then erases the whole thing and starts again. His supervisor asked yesterday if he was sleeping. He said yes. The lie came easily—easier than the truth, which is that sleep vanished eight months ago, replaced by a kind of watchfulness that never stops.

He was twenty-one, finishing his final year of university, living alone in a small apartment near campus. The man was someone he had matched with online—polite, older, patient in their messages. They agreed to meet at his place late on a Thursday night. He remembers the careful way the man folded his jacket over a chair, the scent of coffee on his breath. They kissed. Then things shifted. The man’s hands became harder, his voice lower, his body heavier. He said no. He said it more than once. He tried to push the weight off. The man did not stop. He remembers the ceiling, a crack in the plaster that looked like a river, and the sound of his own breathing—shallow, fast, wrong. Afterward, the man left without speaking. He lay on the floor for a long time.

He did not go to the hospital. He did not tell anyone. The word itself—rape—would not form in his mind for weeks. When it finally did, it felt foreign, like a language he was not supposed to speak. His family is proud, traditional, Middle Eastern. Men in his family do not get raped. Men in his family do not talk about what happens in bedrooms. So he cleaned the sheets, deleted the conversation, and went to his morning class as if the night had never happened.

But the night kept happening.

He will be in a meeting, reviewing quarterly reports, and suddenly he is back on the floor, staring at the crack in the ceiling. The numbers dissolve. He grips the edge of his chair until his knuckles go white. At night, he checks the locks on his door four times before he can sit still. He stopped seeing anyone—friends, family, dates. The thought of someone touching him, even a hand on his shoulder, makes his stomach turn. He told his parents he was busy with work. They seemed relieved; they had been asking when he would find a wife.

At the office, he avoids the break room at certain hours. A coworker once stood too close behind him while he was filing, and he swung around, heart hammering, fists half-raised. He apologized. Said he had not slept. The coworker laughed it off. But he sees the way people look at him now—sidelong glances, careful distances. He knows he is becoming strange. He cannot explain why. The story is trapped inside him, sealed behind a door he cannot open. Sometimes he hears the man’s voice in his head, calm and final, telling him to be quiet. He stays quiet.

He still goes to work. He sits in his cubicle. He moves numbers from one column to another. But nothing adds up anymore. The world feels tilted, like the floor of his apartment tilting at night when he lies awake, listening for footsteps that are not there. He is waiting, always waiting, for something to end or begin—he does not know which.
